title: Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
summary:
A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support.
And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.
Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.
It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.
Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie.

title: What is climate change? A really simple guide
summary:
Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.
The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.
2024 was Earth's hottest year on record, with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.
Temperatures remained high in 2025, despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La Niña.
The opposite El Niño pattern, combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.

title: North Pennines National Landscape prepares for climate change
summary:
Climate change readiness and helping people access the countryside are among priorities in a five-year plan for a national landscape.
The North Pennines National Landscape Management Plan 2026-31 has been adopted by the Cumberland, Westmorland and Furness, County Durham and Northumberland councils.
Chris Woodley-Stewart, director of the North Pennines National Landscape (NPNL), said: "In many ways, its the most ambitious plan that we've ever had, but also the most realistic."
National landscapes were formerly known as areas of outstanding natural beauty, and the North Pennines features heather moors, dales, woods and one of England's highest waterfalls High Force.
One of the priorities in its management plan announced last month was adapting to "warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers".

title: How climate change worsens heatwaves, droughts, fires and floods
summary:
Scientists use computer models to simulate how individual extreme weather events unfold in two scenarios:today's world with about 1.4C, external of human-caused warminga hypothetical world without human influence on the climateThat way, they can estimate, external how much a particular heatwave, storm or drought was affected by climate change.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Five widespread heatwaves affected the country, resulting in 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).
Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy, described summer 2026 as "remarkable" and warned that extreme heat events would only become more common as the world warms.

title: Could the earliest weakening of the polar vortex on record bring UK snow?
summary:
High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.
But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.
While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.
Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.
However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.

title: The polar vortex is weakening unusually early. Here's what that could mean for the weather.
summary:
The polar vortex is weakening unusually early, forecasters have said, with a rare disruption possible within days that could send Arctic air traveling south over North America.
The polar vortex is a band of powerful winds in the stratosphere that circle the North Pole each winter.
"There is no cause to be alarmed when you hear about the polar vortex, but you should be prepared for colder temperatures," its guidance said.
Why is the polar vortex weakening so early?
The earliest polar vortex weakening previously recorded was Nov. 28, 1968.

title: Uganda tree-planting scheme loses Welsh government funding
summary:
The Welsh government will end funding for a tree-planting scheme in Uganda that was branded "woke" by opposition politicians.
Wales has given more than £4m to climate change charity Size of Wales since 2015, to work with Indigenous communities to plant trees in the African nation.
Ministers said budgetary pressures meant "difficult decisions" had to be made and the charity would lose its grant for the scheme at the end of March 2027.
Size of Wales, external works with Indigenous and local people worldwide to grow trees and protect at least two million hectares of tropical forests - an area the size of Wales.
The scheme, funded by previous Labour-run Welsh governments, has seen more than 25 million planted around Mbale in the Mount Elgon region of eastern Uganda.

title: Plastic pollution is putting an old legal doctrine to a new test
summary:
As far as the state’s public nuisance law is concerned, a company’s liability ends at the point of sale.
And can public nuisance laws succeed in making polluters pay?
The notion of public nuisance dates to 13th-century English common law and traditionally applied to violations of rights shared by the public, such as access to clean air.
California, on the other hand, is not, and courts there have so far proven more receptive to plastics public nuisance suits.
Whatever their ultimate outcome in court, Lytton said plastics lawsuits can “win” in other ways — by unearthing new documents, for example, and putting the plastics issue higher on the public-policy agenda.
